title: Love, the path
hook: love is the path the Tenth Guru said finds the Lord

segments.voice: Yesterday, compassion in practice: in the Japji, the bull is dharma, and dharma's mother is daya. Your line was compassion first. Whose load did you ask about before judging them? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-eight.

A heron stands in shallow water at the edge of a pond. Perfectly still. One leg tucked up, eyes half closed, neck curved like a monk bowing in prayer. From the bank, it looks perfectly at peace. Then a fish swims near, and the stillness ends in a flash. It was never meditating. It was waiting for lunch. Guru Gobind Singh, the Tenth Guru, used that bird in a verse. He asked what all our holy-looking stillness is worth, and then gave one answer, plainly, to everyone listening. Today's word is that answer: prem.
screen: `A HERON, STILL AS A MONK.` → `WAITING FOR A FISH.` → `PREM.`

segments.voice: First, the heron. In the Tav Prasad Swayye, which Sikhs recite among their morning prayers, the Tenth Guru asks, in paraphrase: what does it matter if you shut your eyes and sit like a heron in meditation? He goes on through other outward feats: wandering from sea to sea to bathe, losing this world and the next along the way. Each one can look holy from the bank. Each one can be a heron. Second, the answer. At the end of the verse, in paraphrase: I tell you the truth, all of you, listen: only those who have loved have found the Lord. In the original, jin prem keeo tin hee prabh paaeio. The word is prem: love. Not ritual first. Not display first. Love. Third, love has a price. Guru Nanak said it too, in a salok kept near the end of the Granth. In paraphrase: if you long to play the game of love, come to my lane with your head on your palm. Once you set foot on this path, give your head and don't hesitate. That's not soft romance. It's love that costs everything and doesn't look back. Fourth, so what does prem do on an ordinary day? It changes the question under a practice. Not, did I pray long enough, or did I look devout, but, was there love in it? A Sikh can recite every bani and still be a heron. Someone can stumble through one line with a full heart and be found. This is not the Guru throwing out discipline; he wrote prayers Sikhs recite in the morning. It's the Guru naming what the discipline is for. Those who loved, found.
screen: `THE HERON: HOLY FROM THE BANK.` · `ONLY THOSE WHO LOVED FOUND THE LORD.` · `YOUR HEAD ON YOUR PALM.` · `WAS THERE LOVE IN IT?` · then, large: `JIN PREM KEEO TIN HEE PRABH PAAEIO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: love someone openly. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you love but rarely say it to. A parent, a sibling, an old friend, a child who's grown. Let their face come. On each in-breath, let their face stay. On each out-breath, send them whatever love is there. Before the bell ends, decide one plain way to show it today: a message, a call, a word said out loud instead of assumed. If you pray, you can hold them before the Lord. The bell holds the time.
Prem. Love; in the Tenth Guru's swayya, the path that finds the Lord, beneath every ritual and every outward show. Today's word.
Your line: those who loved, found. Today, say the love out loud to the person you chose, plainly, without waiting for a reason. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: The Tav Prasad Swayye is among the morning prayers Sikhs recite, and the line on love, jin prem keeo tin hee prabh paaeio, is sung in kirtan.

fork.setup: you're watching a heron, perfectly still in the water, eyes half closed. what is it doing?
fork.reveal: the Guru's point: holy-looking stillness can be a heron's. only those who have loved have found the Lord.

original.note: Gurmukhi: prem, love, the word in jin prem keeo tin hee prabh paaeio.

trapdoor: what you thought: love is a nice feeling that comes after religion.
what it means: in the Tenth Guru's verse, love is the path itself; outward show can be a heron's stillness.
what a scholar hears: the Tav Prasad Swayye sets the heron beside jin prem keeo tin hee prabh paaeio, echoing Guru Nanak's head-on-the-palm salok.

sources.ref: Tav Prasad Swayye (Akal Ustat, Guru Gobind Singh): kahaa bhaio jo dou lochan moond kai baith rahio bak dhiaan lagaaio ... saach kahoon sun leho sabhai jin prem keeo tin hee prabh paaeio
Ang 1412 (Salok Vaaraan te Vadheek, Guru Nanak: jau tau prem khelan kaa chaao, sir dhar talee galee meree aao)

notes: Please confirm the heron (bak dhiaan) swayya and that 'jin prem keeo tin hee prabh paaeio' closes that same swayya; if the heron image belongs to a neighboring swayya, adjust the teach.

Editor: the list of outward feats now follows the swayya (bathing in the seas, losing this world and the next) instead of adding 'long austerities' it doesn't name; 'on a Tuesday' (day 1384) became 'on an ordinary day'; the practice no longer tells the listener the love is already there. Day 1395's hunter-bowing warning is a near angle; the heron is kept because it is the cited text.
